body:
#### Reference issue
gh-21833

#### What does this implement/fix?
This activate SPEC 7 warnings. SciPy 2.0.0 is the right time to do it because it may be noisy.

#### Additional information
There are some comments in the code that I need to remove and turn into more general questions for discussion.

In implementations, calls to functions that are beginning to emit warnings should generally preserve those calls so as not to change behavior before the deprecation expires; warnings are silenced with `catch_warnings`. There are a few exceptions:
- `scipy.stats.fit` currently provides a default `optimizer` (`differential_evolution`) without passing it an `rng` argument. If `np.random.seed` is set, using this unseeded optimizer would lead to `FutureWarning`s about the use of global random state, but it would not be obvious what the user needs to do to avoid the warning. I'm not sure that we *want* users to feel the need to override `optimizer` just to provide a random state explicitly, and I don't think we want `fit` to accept an `rng` only to pass it along to the default optimizer. So I think the best option is to just change to using `rng=None` and breaking the dependence on global random state immediately rather than later. We can document this as a backward-incompatible change in SciPy 2.0; this seems like a low-impact change, especially for a major release.
- Something similar happens in the `sobol_indices`'s `SobolResult.bootsrap`, which calls `scipy.statsbootstrap` without a seed. I've suggested adding an `rng` argument to ``SobolResult.bootstrap`, which would default to `None`. Again, this is an immediate but minor backward-incompatibility that we can document.
- Same story for `scipy.stats.sampling.FastGeneratorInversion.qrvs` . If no `qmc_engine` is provided, it prepares a `Halton` object with `seed=seed`. This would warn about use of keyword argument of `seed` in a private function, so I've switched to using `rng`. I'm not sure what to do about this one, since it's probably a more significant break. Where the results of `fit` and `sobol_indices` are only mildly dependent on the random state, the whole point of providing `random_state` to `FastGeneratorInversion.qrvs` is to control the output. I'll open a separate issue about this so we do not need to hold up this whole PR.

title: `scipy.linalg`: low-level batch support vs `numpy.linalg`

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: A new feature or improvement

labels.name: RFC
labels.description: Request for Comments; typically used to gather feedback for a substantial change proposal

body:
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/21466 added support for batched ND arrays across `scipy.linalg`. This effort was mostly completed in the scipy 1.16.x timeframe.
In the 1.17 and 1.18 window, we moved several functions to low-level C code. This improves performance, esp for batches of small matrices, at a cost of more complicated code---which is worse maintenance-wise.
Therefore, we do not necessarily want to move all batch looping to native code. This issue is to prioritize which parts of `scipy.linalg` need looping in C, and which can stay in python.

One relevant aspect is the duplication between `scipy.linalg` and `numpy.linalg`. Typically, scipy functions have more features, and numpy functions are faster, partly because their batch support is all in C. 

So a first shot at a North Start goal could be to _make scipy.linalg a strict superset of numpy.linalg_. This is not very realistic or even desirable. First, there are difficult backwards compatibility considerations (e.g. https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/4818); Second, why would we even bother implementing `scipy.linalg.trace`.

So an amended goal: _for each function which is in both scipy.linalg and numpy.linalg, the scipy version has all features of the numpy version, may have additional features, and has a comparable performance_.

With this in mind, here's a listing of https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/routines.linalg.html, with an opinionated prioritization (a filled checkbox means already implemented):

**Matrix and vector products**

`dot`, `outer`, `cross`, `einsum` etc : out of scope for `scipy.linalg`.

**Decompositions**

- [x] `cholesky`
- [x]  `qr`
- [x] `svd`
- [x] `svdvals`

**Matrix eigenvalues**

- [x] `eig`
- [x] `eigvals`
- [x] `eigh`
- [x] `eigvalsh`

**Solving equations and inverting matrices**

- [x] `solve`
- [x] `inv`
- [x] `lstsq`
- [x] `pinv`
- `tensorsolve`, `tensorinv`  : out of scope


**Norms and other numbers**

Mostly out of scope. Potentially in-scope:

- [x] `det`
`det` is rather low priority. Our implementation goes to significant lengths for numerical stability (I think?), so we should check if our implementation is more stable than numpy's. If it is, maybe consider porting our improvements to numpy instead. 
- [ ] `norm`
<s>I think `norm` is rather low priority</s>. If we ever get to it, we should introduce `vector_norm` and `matrix_norm`, like numpy did, and only if we plan to offer some norms that numpy does not.

**Other matrix operations**

- `diagonal`, `matrix_transpose` : out of scope

-------------------------

Out of unchecked boxes, the obvious high-priority item is `eigh`. It is frequently used, and scipy's version has quite a few bells and whistles compared to numpy's. It's not entirely clear though which of them are in common use and which ones are historical artefacts (`subset_by_index`?).

title: BUG: sparse.linalg.cg falsely reports success when true residual misses tolerance by 70 million times

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
### Describe your issue.

When running the cg solver with a large initial guess, the internal recursive residual can drift wildly from the true residual due to floating point precision limits.

Because of this, the solver returns info=0 (success), even though the actual mathematical residual (b - A @ x) exceeds the requested tolerance by a massive factor. In the reproducer given below, the solver declares success despite the true residual missing the requested target by approximately 70,000,000x.

I have a locally tested candidate patch that solves this by confirming convergence using a fresh b - A @ x matvec before returning 0. I would be happy to open a PR with this approach for maintainer review.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse.linalg import cg

A = np.diag([1., 1e10])
b = np.ones(2)

# Start with a very large initial guess
x, info = cg(A, b, x0=np.full(2, 1e6), rtol=1e-8, atol=0)

residual = np.linalg.norm(b - A @ x)
limit = 1e-8 * np.linalg.norm(b)

print(f"info: {info}") # Returns 0 (Success)
print(f"true_residual: {residual}") # Returns 1.0
print(f"limit: {limit}") # Returns 1.414e-08
```

### Error message

```shell
No exception is raised. The solver silently returns success (info=0) despite a massive tolerance violation:

Observed output: info: 0 true_residual: 1.0 limit: 1.414213562373095e-08
```

```shell
Windows 11
Python 3.14.2
SciPy 1.18.1
NumPy 2.5.3
```

title: BUG: stats: bivariate normal CDF reads the upper triangle of the covariance matrix

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
The documentation for [`scipy.stats.multivariate_normal`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.multivariate_normal.html) states that

```markdown
Symmetry is not checked; only the lower triangular portion is used.
```

However, the bivariate normal CDF reads an upper-triangular entry (see below)

https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/1b72b285a89b5932a59e9ad9e64327d79f1d9b8f/scipy/stats/_qmvnt.py#L491

Hence, we have

```python
from scipy.stats import multivariate_normal

A = [[1.0, 0.5], [0.5, 1.0]]

# Same covariance entries in the lower triangle; upper triangle omitted.
# not Cholesky factor
B = [[1.0, 0.0], [0.5, 1.0]]

print(multivariate_normal.cdf([0.0, 0.0], cov=A))
# Approximately 0.3333333333333333

print(multivariate_normal.cdf([0.0, 0.0], cov=B))
# 0.25

print(multivariate_normal.cdf([0.0, 0.0], cov=np.array(B).T))
# Approximately 0.3333333333333333
```

If we agree this is indeed a bug, I'll submit a PR fixing this.

I found this while working on adding a trivariate CDF fast path from https://github.com/scipy/xsf/pull/270

title: BUG: stats.ttest_ind / special.stdtr returns zero for a representable subnormal Student-t tail

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
### Describe your issue.

In SciPy 1.18.1, a Welch two-sample t-test returns a two-sided p-value of 0.0 even though the mathematical probability is approximately 3.504710110487091e-316, a positive value representable as binary64 (3.5047101e-316). The test statistic and degrees of freedom are correct. No warning is emitted.

Each group has 201 ordinary, exactly representable observations: x contains 100 copies of -1, one 0, and 100 copies of 1; y = x + 12. Their means are 0 and 12, and both unbiased sample variances are exactly 1. Thus the Welch statistic is -12/sqrt(2/201), with t² = 14472 and df = 400.

For this case, the exact two-sided probability is the regularized incomplete beta value

I_{400/(400+14472)}(200, 1/2) = I_{50/1859}(200, 1/2) ≈ 3.5047101104870913387606868475703e-316.

An independent positive-term series calculation agrees with the high-precision incomplete-beta result. Simple bounds from 1 ≤ (1-u)^(-1/2) ≤ (1-z)^(-1/2) over 0 ≤ u ≤ z, with z=50/1859, give 3.457494873756592e-316 < p < 3.504951044561724e-316. In particular, this is not a probability that must round to zero in binary64.

The same reproducer returns 3.5047101e-316 in SciPy 1.16.1, but 0.0 in 1.17.0 and 1.18.1. In 1.18.1, stats.t.sf(abs(t), 400) and special.stdtr(400, -abs(t)) also return zero (their one-sided reference probability is half the value above). This places the observed zero at or below the Student-t CDF calculation; I have not established a more specific internal cause.

Related but distinct reports: #26169 concerns Welch degrees of freedom under extreme rescaling; #25667 concerns stdtr accuracy near the center of the distribution for df=1. A limited Issue/PR search found no exact duplicate of this subnormal tail example.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import warnings

import numpy as np
import scipy
from scipy import special, stats

x = np.r_[np.full(100, -1.0), 0.0, np.full(100, 1.0)]
y = x + 12.0

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    result = stats.ttest_ind(x, y, equal_var=False)
    sf = stats.t.sf(abs(result.statistic), result.df)
    cdf = special.stdtr(result.df, -abs(result.statistic))

print("SciPy:", scipy.__version__, "NumPy:", np.__version__)
print("Welch:", result)
print("one-sided sf:", sf, "stdtr:", cdf)
print("warnings:", [str(w.message) for w in caught])


Independent reference (requires `mpmath`; does not call SciPy):


from mpmath import mp

mp.dps = 130
z = mp.mpf(50) / 1859
a = 200
reference = mp.betainc(a, mp.mpf("0.5"), 0, z, regularized=True)
series = mp.fsum(
    mp.binomial(2*k, k) * z**(a+k) / (mp.power(4, k) * (a+k))
    for k in range(100)
) / mp.beta(a, mp.mpf("0.5"))

print(mp.nstr(reference, 40))
print(mp.nstr(series, 40))
print(float(reference))
```

### Error message

```shell
SciPy: 1.18.1 NumPy: 2.3.5
Welch: TtestResult(statistic=np.float64(-120.29962593458053), pvalue=np.float64(0.0), df=np.float64(400.0))
one-sided sf: 0.0 stdtr: 0.0
warnings: []


The reference converts to `3.5047101e-316` as a Python binary64 float. SciPy 1.16.1 returned that positive two-sided value for the same inputs; SciPy 1.17.0 also returned zero.
```

### SciPy/NumPy/Python version and system information

```shell
Reproduced with SciPy 1.18.1, NumPy 2.3.5, Python 3.12.14, Linux x86-64 (glibc 2.39). The version comparison used SciPy 1.16.1 and 1.17.0 in the same Python environment. The current development-branch binary has not been tested.
```

title: BUG: sparse.csgraph: handle duplicate CSR entries in bipartite matching

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Items that need further discussion before they are merged or closed

labels.name: Cython
labels.description: Issues with the internal Cython code base

body:
#### Reference issue

Closes gh-26160

#### What does this implement/fix?

`maximum_bipartite_matching`, `structural_rank` and
`min_weight_full_bipartite_matching` crash (or hang, or return garbage) when the CSR input stores the same entry more than once. `_hopcroft_karp` in `scipy/sparse/csgraph/_matching.pyx` pushes `y[u]` onto a fixed-size DFS stack once for every stored entry that passes the level check, so a row stored `K` times pushes the same row `K` times. The stack has only `i + 1` slots and the extension is compiled with `boundscheck(False)`, so the extra pushes overwrite heap memory.

CSR arrays may legitimately contain duplicate entries — `tocsr()` does not always merge them, and `eliminate_zeros()` / `.T.tocsr()` keep them. A `coo` input is not affected because converting to CSR merges duplicates.

**Changes**

- `scipy/sparse/csgraph/_matching.pyx`:
  - `maximum_bipartite_matching`: merge duplicate entries (copy + `sum_duplicates`) when the input has no canonical format, before calling `_hopcroft_karp`.
  - `min_weight_full_bipartite_matching`: same normalization, before the feasibility search and `_lapjvsp`. Duplicate weights are summed, matching scipy's standard semantics for duplicates.
- `structural_rank` (in `_reordering.pyx`) delegates to `maximum_bipartite_matching`, so it is covered automatically.
- Tests added in `scipy/sparse/csgraph/tests/test_matching.py` for all three functions using `K = 100_000` duplicate entries, which overflow the stack on every platform before this fix.

**Why this approach**

Canonicalizing the input keeps the documented space complexity of `_hopcroft_karp` ($O(|E| \sqrt{|V|})$ time, linear in the number of rows) and also protects `_lapjvsp` (which reads the same arrays in `min_weight_full_bipartite_matching`); growing the stack to `nnz + 1` would break the space guarantee and leave `_lapjvsp` exposed.

#### Verification

- Pre-fix behavior of the issue's reproducer on SciPy 1.18.1 (Python 3.14, Linux):
  - `maximum_bipartite_matching`: **segmentation fault** (exit 139)
  - `structural_rank`: **hang** (no completion within 20 s)
  - `min_weight_full_bipartite_matching`: **segmentation fault** (exit 139)
- Post-fix: same input is normalized to a canonical 3-entry CSR, and the searches return the correct maximum matching (both partitions), structural rank 2, and a valid full matching M-bM-^@M-^T verified on the compiled extension by canonicalizing before the search, mirroring exactly what the added two-line wrappers do.
- The edited `_matching.pyx` passes a full Cython compile.
- Full from-source build (meson + OpenBLAS, Cython 3.3.0) of the branch: `test_matching.py` 37 passed; `scipy/sparse/csgraph/tests/` 1350 passed, 58 skipped; CSR/CSC ABI smoke 37 passed, 1 skipped.

#### Additional information

The pre-fix and patched `_matching.pyx` variants were each compiled with Cython and hot-swapped in place, so the crash signatures above come from the real compiled extension rather than an emulation. Review responses are in the thread above.

#### AI Generation Disclosure

AI assistance was used in the preparation of this pull request.

- **Tool:** the `big-pickle` model (model ID `opencode/big-pickle`), used through the `opencode` command-line coding agent.
- **How it was used:** to analyse the stack overflow in `_hopcroft_karp` and identify the duplicate-entry push pattern, to implement the normalization guards in `scipy/sparse/csgraph/_matching.pyx`, to write the regression tests in `scipy/sparse/csgraph/tests/test_matching.py`, and to produce the before/after verification (including compiling and hot-swapping pre-fix and patched `_matching.pyx` variants to obtain the real crash signatures).

#### Reference issue
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/24148#issuecomment-5284580100

#### What does this implement/fix?
Previously, the `_apply_over_batch` would only validate input shapes if an input had zero size.
This changes it to perform the input validation on all input.

For instance, `solve_sylvester(np.eye(2), np.eye(3), np.eye(2))` raises the following in `main`:

```
ValueError: shapes (2,2) and (3,3) not aligned:
2 (dim 1) != 3 (dim 0)
```

With this PR:
```
ValueError: The core shape(s) of the array argument(s):
a: (2, 2), b: (3, 3), q: (2, 2)
is/are incompatible with the shapes in the signature:
a: (i, i), b: (j, j), q: (i, j)
```
Of course, we could add additional logic to make the error as specific as we like.

Even if functions had readable error messages to begin with, this makes the messages consistent so users only have to learn to interpret one type of message. As an added benefit, we could now delete a ton of of function-specific input validation code.

The PR also explains NEP 5 signatures in the `linalg` batch tutorial and fixes some bugs.

#### Additional information 
If we don't want to turn this on for all functions, we can add an option to `_apply_over_batch` to opt in to the input validation. In any case, there's a lot of other little improvements in this PR.

body:
#### Reference issue

Closes gh-26160. Alternative to gh-26242.

#### What does this implement/fix?

Duplicate sparse entries can push the same row repeatedly onto the fixed-size stack in `_hopcroft_karp`. Use the existing `parents` array to push each child only once from a given row. Reset the parents at each BFS phase. This keeps the stack bounded by the row count and leaves unexplored siblings available for later augmenting paths in the same phase. The unweighted search keeps its input unchanged and requires no additional array.

For weighted matching, sum duplicate weights on the copy already created by `astype`, before removing zero weights. This also prevents an independent overflow in the `todo` array in `_lapjvsp_single_l`. Preserve the compressed format when casting index arrays, so rectangular CSC inputs with 64-bit indices remain valid.

Add regression tests for CSR, CSC, and COO inputs, unsorted duplicates, explicit-zero edges, input preservation, both index widths, rectangular graphs, minimization and maximization, and duplicate weights that cancel.

#### AI Generation Disclosure
No AI yet except that I had GPT-5.6 Sol analyze a log of all the `shapes`, `x_shape`, and `y_shape` generated by `draw_distribution_from_family` (main vs PR) to check that we're still getting good coverage. Turns out we're getting better coverage just with randomness, and parametrizing over `shape_options` gives us more control to add specific cases.

<details>

# Shape and broadcasting coverage: `main.npz` versus `PR2.npz`

## Executive summary

`PR2.npz` is much more effective at generating distinct, nontrivial broadcasting configurations within ranks 0 through 3. Despite containing five fewer records, it has 1,543 distinct exact configurations, compared with 888 in `main.npz`. It also uses scalars less often and makes two or more operands broadcast in 93.2% of records, compared with 74.4% in `main.npz`.

`main.npz` has one important advantage: it covers higher dimensionality. Its results reach rank 6, whereas every result in `PR2.npz` has rank at most 3. Consequently, `main.npz` has a larger raw vocabulary of shapes, but much of that advantage comes from ranks 4 through 6 rather than denser coverage at ordinary ranks.

The strongest combined strategy would use PR2-style generation for ranks 0 through 3 and retain a small, deliberate set of rank-4 through rank-6 cases.

## Data and methodology

Each record was normalized to

```text
(tuple(parameter_shapes), x_shape, y_shape)
```

NumPy integer dimensions were converted to Python integers before comparisons. All parameter shapes, the `x` shape, and the `y` shape were treated as separate broadcasting operands. The broadcast-result shape was computed with `numpy.broadcast_shapes`.

The archives contain only shape information. They do not identify the distribution or operation associated with each record. Therefore, two records with the same shapes may still test different implementations. Counts of duplicates in this report measure duplication of shape configurations, not necessarily redundant tests.

## Definitions

The short labels used below have the following precise meanings.

**Exact configuration**

The complete ordered combination of all parameter shapes, the `x` shape, and the `y` shape. Parameter order is significant. Two records are exact duplicates only when all these shapes agree.

**Structural broadcast pattern**

A configuration after discarding the particular values of ordinary dimensions while retaining:

- the number of parameter operands;
- every operand's rank;
- operand order;
- on every aligned axis, whether each operand has a missing leading axis, dimension zero, dimension one, or an ordinary dimension greater than one.

Thus, structurally equivalent examples such as `(2, 1)` with `(1, 3)` and `(4, 1)` with `(1, 2)` count as the same pattern. Zero is kept distinct because zero-length broadcasting has special behavior.

**Implicit leading-axis expansion** or **rank padding**

At least one operand has fewer axes than the broadcast result. NumPy aligns shapes from the right, which is equivalent to prepending dimensions of size one to the shorter operand. A scalar broadcasting to any nonscalar result is included in this category.

**Mixed operand ranks**

Not all operands have the same rank. For these mutually broadcastable records, this is equivalent to saying that at least one operand undergoes implicit leading-axis expansion.

**Singleton expansion**

At least one explicit input dimension of size one aligns with a result dimension that is not one. This includes both ordinary cases such as `1 -> 4` and zero-length cases such as `1 -> 0`. Merely prepending an implicit dimension to a shorter operand does not by itself count as singleton expansion.

**No broadcasting required**

Every operand shape is already exactly equal to the result shape. This is stricter than merely saying that the shapes are mutually broadcastable. For example, `()` with `(3,)` does require broadcasting under this definition.

**Operand changed to the result shape**

An operand's original shape is not exactly equal to the broadcast-result shape. This includes changes caused by rank padding, singleton expansion, or both. It describes logical shape expansion; it does not imply that NumPy materializes a copied array.

**Zero-length dimension present**

At least one operand has an explicit dimension of size zero. Because every record is mutually broadcastable, the corresponding result axis is also zero-length.

**Zero against singleton**

On at least one aligned axis, one operand has an explicit zero and another has an explicit one. Missing leading axes do not count as explicit singleton dimensions for this metric. For example, `(0, 3)` with `(1, 3)` qualifies and broadcasts to `(0, 3)`.

**Same-rank, multidirectional singleton expansion**

At least two nonscalar operands have the same rank as the result and expand explicit singleton dimensions on different axes. For example, `(3, 1)` with `(1, 4)` broadcasts to `(3, 4)`: the first operand expands on the second axis and the second operand expands on the first.

**Three operands owning different result axes**

At least three distinct operands uniquely provide ordinary dimensions greater than one on three distinct result axes. On each such axis, the other operands have either a singleton dimension or a missing leading axis. A canonical example is `(2, 1, 1)`, `(1, 3, 1)`, and `(1, 1, 4)`, which broadcast to `(2, 3, 4)`.

**All operands scalar**

Every parameter shape, the `x` shape, and the `y` shape is `()`.

## Overall diversity

| Metric | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---|---:|---:|
| Records | 2,025 | 2,020 |
| Distinct exact configurations | 888 (43.9%) | 1,543 (76.4%) |
| Repeated records by exact shape | 1,137 | 477 |
| Largest multiplicity of one exact configuration | 232 | 49 |
| Distinct structural broadcast patterns | 877 | 1,223 |
| Distinct input shapes across all roles | 269 | 155 |
| Distinct broadcast-result shapes | 273 | 156 |

PR2 produces 655 more distinct exact configurations with five fewer records. Its lower raw count of distinct shapes is explained by its rank cap: PR2 draws from a compact rank-0-through-rank-3 universe, while main reaches rank 6.

The most common exact configuration in both archives is the one-parameter all-scalar case:

```text
parameter shapes = [()], x = (), y = () -> result = ()
```

It occurs 232 times in main and 49 times in PR2.

## Rank coverage

### Broadcast-result ranks

| Result rank | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 448 (22.1%) | 69 (3.4%) |
| 1 | 315 (15.6%) | 301 (14.9%) |
| 2 | 659 (32.5%) | 619 (30.6%) |
| 3 | 223 (11.0%) | 1,031 (51.0%) |
| 4 | 298 (14.7%) | 0 |
| 5 | 42 (2.1%) | 0 |
| 6 | 40 (2.0%) | 0 |

Main assigns 18.8% of its records to result ranks 4 through 6. PR2 instead concentrates just over half of its records at rank 3.

### Distinct input shapes by rank

| Input-shape rank | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` | Possible in PR2's `{0,1,2,3,4}` dimension universe |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 1 | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| 2 | 21 | 25 | 25 |
| 3 | 60 | 124 | 125 |
| 4 | 110 | 0 | Not in scope |
| 5 | 34 | 0 | Not in scope |
| 6 | 38 | 0 | Not in scope |

PR2 covers every possible rank-0, rank-1, and rank-2 input shape using dimensions `{0,1,2,3,4}`. At rank 3 it covers 124 of 125 possibilities; the only absent input shape is `(2, 2, 0)`. That shape does occur as a broadcast result, so PR2 still covers all 156 possible result shapes in its bounded universe.

## Coverage by operand role

| Role | Metric | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Parameters | Operand occurrences | 3,370 | 3,360 |
| Parameters | Distinct shapes | 13 | 148 |
| Parameters | Scalar occurrences | 1,921 (57.0%) | 1,426 (42.4%) |
| `x` | Operand occurrences | 2,025 | 2,020 |
| `x` | Distinct shapes | 143 | 139 |
| `x` | Scalar occurrences | 929 (45.9%) | 539 (26.7%) |
| `y` | Operand occurrences | 2,025 | 2,020 |
| `y` | Distinct shapes | 219 | 115 |
| `y` | Scalar occurrences | 1,042 (51.5%) | 558 (27.6%) |

The most substantial PR2 improvement is parameter-shape diversity: 148 distinct shapes rather than 13. Main's larger `y` vocabulary is primarily a consequence of permitting ranks 4 through 6.

Across all roles, 52.5% of main's operands are scalar, compared with 34.1% of PR2's operands.

## Broadcasting mechanisms

| Per-record condition | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---|---:|---:|
| No broadcasting required | 453 (22.4%) | 76 (3.8%) |
| Implicit leading-axis expansion, without singleton expansion | 872 (43.1%) | 750 (37.1%) |
| Singleton expansion, without implicit leading-axis expansion | 2 (0.1%) | 46 (2.3%) |
| Both mechanisms | 698 (34.5%) | 1,148 (56.8%) |
| Any implicit leading-axis expansion | 1,570 (77.5%) | 1,898 (94.0%) |
| Any singleton expansion | 700 (34.6%) | 1,194 (59.1%) |
| Zero-length dimension present | 728 (36.0%) | 705 (34.9%) |

The four mechanism rows at the top of the table are mutually exclusive and exhaust all records. PR2's main improvement is not merely that it broadcasts more often: it combines rank padding and explicit singleton expansion in 56.8% of records, compared with 34.5% in main.

### Number of operands changed to the result shape

| Changed operands | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 453 (22.4%) | 76 (3.8%) |
| 1 | 65 (3.2%) | 61 (3.0%) |
| 2 | 451 (22.3%) | 711 (35.2%) |
| 3 | 749 (37.0%) | 798 (39.5%) |
| 4 | 307 (15.2%) | 374 (18.5%) |

Records have either three operands (one parameter, `x`, and `y`) or four operands (two parameters, `x`, and `y`). PR2 changes at least two operands in 1,883 records, or 93.2% of the archive. Main does so in 1,507 records, or 74.4%.

## Selected situations

| Situation | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---|---:|---:|
| Same-rank, multidirectional singleton expansion | 12 | 38 |
| Three operands owning different result axes | 3 | 2 |
| Zero against singleton | 359 | 399 |
| All operands scalar | 448 | 69 |

Both archives contain every selected situation. PR2 gives substantially more coverage to same-rank multidirectional expansion and slightly more to explicit zero-versus-singleton broadcasting. Cases in which three operands independently determine three result axes remain rare in both archives.

The all-scalar count is large in main because it includes records associated with different parameter counts and, potentially, different distributions. It should not automatically be interpreted as 448 redundant tests. As shape coverage alone, however, it is heavy repetition of the same baseline condition.

## Dimension values

Counting every explicit axis in every operand:

| Dimension value | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1,273 | 1,168 |
| 1 | 4,221 | 4,730 |
| 2 | 1,122 | 1,213 |
| 3 | 304 | 1,270 |
| 4 | 89 | 1,254 |
| 5 | 8 | 0 |

On non-singleton ordinary dimensions, PR2 is much more balanced across sizes 2, 3, and 4. Main is strongly concentrated on size 2 and uses size 5 only eight times. The high frequency of ones in both archives is expected for generators designed to produce mutually broadcastable shapes.

## Assessment

Within ranks 0 through 3, PR2 is the stronger suite by a wide margin. It provides:

- many more exact and structural configurations;
- nearly exhaustive coverage of its intended input-shape universe;
- dramatically broader parameter-shape coverage;
- fewer all-scalar and otherwise non-broadcasting records;
- more cases combining rank padding with explicit singleton expansion; and
- more cases in which several operands change shape simultaneously.

Main remains valuable for a separate reason: high-rank coverage. It has 380 records whose broadcast result has rank 4, 5, or 6, including 82 at ranks 5 and 6. PR2 tests none of these ranks.

If PR2 is intended to replace main entirely, loss of high-rank coverage is the principal regression. If high-rank behavior is not inherently important, PR2 is a clear improvement. body:
Closes gh-10294.

#### What does this implement/fix?
For every method except `lm`, `scipy.optimize.root` requires `fun` to return as
many elements as `x0`. When this was violated, the solvers failed with
confusing, method-specific errors (e.g. hybr's "array returned by a function
changed size between calls", "cannot reshape array of size N into shape ()",
krylov's "expected square matrix").

This validates the sizes on the solver's own first residual evaluation and
raises a single, clear `ValueError` that points users to `method='lm'` when a
rectangular system is intended. `lm` is exempt because it solves a least-squares
problem. The requirement is now also documented in the `fun` parameter
description. Because the check reuses the existing residual evaluation, it adds
no extra function calls and uses each method's own array convention, so 2-D
`x0` inputs continue to work. Regression tests are added in
`scipy/optimize/tests/test__root.py`.

#### Additional information
The check runs on the first residual evaluation; a `fun` that changes its output
size only on later calls is still caught by the solvers' existing "changed size
between calls" guard.

title: ENH: interpolate.make_smoothing_spline: support GCV algorithm for user defined knots

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: A new feature or improvement

body:
#### Reference issue
Part 2 of gh-25862. That PR added support for user-provided knots `t` with an explicit `lam`, this one adds automatic `lam` selection via GCV, so `lam=None` works for user knots the same way it does for the default knots.

#### What does this implement/fix?
This PR adapts the Generalized Cross Validation algorithm for the case when user passes the knot vector. The previous GCV path assumed that knots are always at the data sites. This PR implements the general case of the GCV algorithm
implementing the formulas defined in [this](https://github.com/aadya940/scipy-bspline-testing/blob/main/B_Splines_with_arbitary_knots-gcv.pdf) companion report Section 12.

#### Additional information

**Design**
- The search is scale-free. We compute the scale `r = tr(XᵀWX) / tr(Ω)` and minimize the GCV criterion over `s = log10(lam / r)` in a fixed bounded window, instead of searching `lam` directly.
- Rescaling `x` or `y` rescales the selected `lam` by exactly the right factor and returns the same spline.
- The window edges match the two failure extremes of the linear system: below it the penalty is under the roundoff of the data term, above it the system is numerically singular. This also avoids the failures of linear-scale search discussed in gh-23472.

**Implementation**
- The influence-matrix trace is computed from the banded Cholesky factor using de Hoog's formula, so each evaluation of the criterion is `O(m)`. No dense inverse is formed.
- Upper-banded (LAPACK) storage is used throughout the user-knots path.
- Solver failures inside the search propagate as `LinAlgError`.
- TODO left in the code: estimate the condition number via LAPACK `dpbcon` once it is wrapped in `scipy.linalg` (separate follow-up PR later).

**Tests**
- Main test: knots at all data sites must reproduce the default GCV path.
- Grid-argmin check of the GCV criterion.
- Auto-selection compared against R's `smooth.spline` with forced knots.
- Weighted data.
- Scale-invariance at scales from `3e-6` to `1e6`.

body:
### Describe your issue.

NumPy 2.2+ allow `RandomState` objects to be wrapped as `Generator`s with `np.random.default_rng`. In many common cases, these are interchangeable. 

```python3
import numpy as np
seed = 9348175
random_state = np.random.RandomState(9348175)
rng = np.random.default_rng(np.random.RandomState(9348175))
print(random_state.random(), rng.random())
# 0.5664197261501696 0.5664197261501696
```

However, I've found two instances that are problematic in SciPy:
- `_rng_spawn` fails when it gets a `RandomState` wrapped as a generator. This affects a lot of things that involve QMC @tupui.
- `rng_integers` produces different values if it gets a `Generator`-wrapped `RandomState` instead of hte original `RandomState`. This affects code in `sparse`, `optimize`, `cluster`, `linalg`, and `stats`.

This is going to create problems when functions begin to standardize `rng` arguments using `np.random.default_rng` instead of `check_random_state`.

This was not a problem when we started the SPEC 7 transition because `RandomState`s could not be wrapped as `Generator`s. In fact, the warnings we wrote for users specifically advised against continued use of `RandomState`s, mentioning that they would result in errors. It's also not NumPy's fault, really, since `_rng_spawn` relies on the private `_bit_generator` attribute of a `Generator`, and `rng_integers` branches based on whether the input is a `Generator` or not.

title: ENH: optimize.bisect: improve worst case performance

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: A new feature or improvement

body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

I come across an interesting point regarding the bisection root finder when browsing @SimpleArt‘s (MIT licensed) project https://github.com/SimpleArt/pyroot. The standard bisection method starts with an initial bracket $[a_0,b_0]$ and repeatedly evaluates the function on $x_{k+1}:=(a_k+b_k)/2$ and shrinks the bracket according to the sign of $f(x_{k+1})$ in the obvious manner.

The author [points out](https://github.com/SimpleArt/pyroot/wiki/Binary-Search) that, when bisecting an independent variable $x$ stored in `float64` format, it is more efficient to bisect the _bit pattern_ of $x$ rather than the _value_ of $x$. For example, given the bracket  $[1,10^{100}]$, rather than checking (roughly) $5\times 10^{99}$, check (roughly) $10^{50}$ instead.

Since $x$ has 64 bits, this strategy ensures 1 ULP precision is attained with no more than 65 function evaluations. This worst case performance is significantly better than the standard bisection method, which would require 1000+ function evaluations in the worst case to achieve 1 ULP accuracy.



### Describe the solution you'd like.

Enrich the `bisect` method with an option to bisect the set of floating point numbers within the initial bracket.

body:
#### Reference issue
This function is one crucial step towards #11291. See also mailing list thread https://mail.python.org/pipermail/scipy-dev/2020-January/023918.html.

#### What does this implement/fix?
This PR adds Wright's generalized Bessel function as `scipy.special.wright_bessel`, see https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.46.E1.

#### Additional information.
~~This is a pure Python implementation that aims for correctness and not for speed.~~ I did not find any public implementation as a reference.
As it is an entire function, the series representation is always valid. ~~I tried asymptotic expansions for large argument z, without any luck.~~

Edit:
So far, only non-negative values of rho=a, beta=b and z=x are implemented. There are 5 different approaches depending on the ranges of the arguments.

1. Taylor series expansion in x=0 [1], for x <= 1.
    Involves gamma funtions in each term.
2. Taylor series expansion in x=0 [2], for large a.
3. Taylor series in a=0, for tiny a and not too large x.
4. Asymptotic expansion for large x [3, 4].
    Suitable for large x while still small a and b.
5. Integral representation [5], in principle for all arguments.


References:
- [1] https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.46.E1
- [2] P. K. Dunn, G. K. Smyth (2005), Series evaluation of Tweedie exponential
     dispersion model densities. Statistics and Computing 15 (2005): 267-280.

     function. Proc. London Math. Soc. (2) 38, pp. 257-270.

title: BUG: sparse.linalg: fix float32 upcast to float64 in norm

labels.name: defect

body:
Fixes gh-26281.

## What is the issue?

`scipy.sparse.linalg.norm` can return `float64` for `float32`
sparse inputs for certain norm orders.

The issue is caused by `np.can_cast(x.dtype, float)` evaluating
to `True` for `float32`, which results in an `astype(float)` cast
and therefore promotes the input to `float64`.

## What does this change?

Replace the broad cast check with:

This keeps the existing promotion behavior for boolean and integer
inputs while preserving the original precision of floating-point
and complex inputs.

## Tests

Added `test_norm_dtype_match` to verify sparse norm output dtypes
against `numpy.linalg.norm` for:

- float32
- float64
- complex64
- complex128

body:
_AI usage declaration: this description is significantly hand-edited from a first draft created by Codex with Astra 6. I started investigating manually after seeing the failures in gh-26284, but that quickly became too much work, so I let Codex do the digging into historical logs and correlating failures with runner types._

[This workflow in `linux.yml`](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/104a82368bc4b4d8b253c97dddc385b9fe48b93b/.github/workflows/linux.yml#L29-L40) intermittently produces hundreds of numerical failures in the two matrix entries of `test_meson`, both using Ubuntu 22.04 and system OpenBLAS `0.3.20+ds-1`:

- `pyrefly (py3.12) & dev deps (py3.15), fast, spin (3.12, false)`
- `pyrefly (py3.12) & dev deps (py3.15), fast, spin (3.15-dev, false)`

The Python 3.12 entry reports 344–347 failures; the Python 3.15-dev entry reports 628–635. Despite the different totals, they share a distinctive failure in `scipy/linalg/tests/test_blas.py::test_trsm[fblas.dtrsm]`, including identical incorrect values. The inspected Python 3.15-dev failures include 342 of the 344 test IDs from an older affected Python 3.12 run. 

The difference between the 3.12 and 3.15 flavors of the job is that currently, the 3.15 version builds `numpy` from source, which causes `numpy` to also be linked against the system OpenBLAS 0.3.20 rather than have its own vendored `scipy-openblas64`.

**Frequency and affected jobs**

In 117 Linux workflow runs on `main` created September 1–26, 2026 (UTC), **10 runs, approximately 8.5%, show this numerical failure signature**:

| Matrix entry | Affected workflow runs | Percentage of all 117 sampled runs | Failure totals |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Python 3.12 (`3.12, false`) | 4 | 3.4% | 344–347 |
| Python 3.15-dev (`3.15-dev, false`) | 6 | 5.1% | 628–635 |
| Either entry | 10 | 8.5% | |

These counts use the latest recorded attempt of each workflow run and exclude PR runs. The denominator includes runs where a matrix entry was cancelled or failed before testing, so this is an observed workflow incidence, not a per-completed-job failure probability. Other CI failures were excluded from the numerator, including dependency-install failures, timeouts, collection errors, and the recent `platformdirs`/xp-marker problem. No matching signature was found in the other failed jobs inspected in this sample. The failures are concentrated in these two matrix entries, rather than scattered across jobs. Matrix cancellation also limits what we can conclude about unaffected siblings.

The four Python 3.12 cases were September 5 (two), September 6, and September 26. The six Python 3.15-dev cases were September 3, September 8 (two), September 12 (two), and September 21.

**Historical examples**

The failure predates the latest runner image and is confirmed as far back as August 12. All affected logs inspected report Azure region `centralus`; the passing comparison logs below report `eastus`.

| Run date / job log | Python entry | Ubuntu 22.04 image | Azure region | Failed tests |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| [August 12](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/actions/runs/31635327432/job/94244118935) | 3.12 | 20260720.234.2 | centralus | 344 |
| [August 18](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/actions/runs/32114407429/job/95640631164) | 3.12 | 20260810.260.1 | centralus | 344 |
| [September 3](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/actions/runs/33742275337/job/100606734614) | 3.15-dev | 20260824.273.3 | centralus | 628 |
| [September 5](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/actions/runs/33961910768/job/101295153365) | 3.12 | 20260831.284.1 | centralus | 344 |
| [September 21](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/actions/runs/35618980715/job/106396995733) | 3.15-dev | 20260907.292.1 | centralus | 635 |
| [September 26, passing](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/actions/runs/36244002972/job/108409694500) | 3.12 | 20260920.303.1 | eastus | 0 |
| [September 26, failing](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/actions/runs/36233646361/job/108381379247) | 3.12 | 20260920.303.1 | centralus | 347 |
| [PR #26284](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/actions/runs/36302374843/job/108572313642) | 3.12 | 20260920.303.1 | centralus | 347 |

**Failure signature**

In the linked PR run, failures span `linalg` (85), `interpolate` (155), `optimize` (52), `sparse` (51), `integrate` (3), and `signal` (1). The `dtrsm` test has substantial errors, not just last-bit differences:

```text
Mismatched elements: 40 / 56 (71.4%)
[0, 2]: -0.9209525326223638 (ACTUAL), -2.063298784417585 (DESIRED)
Max absolute difference among violations: 4.13441317
Max relative difference among violations: 11.85676304
```

All 344 failing test IDs from the older Python 3.12 logs occur in the recent 347-failure log. The additional three are `test_gbcon[1-float64]`, `test_gbcon[I-float64]`, and `test_gbcon[O-float64]`, whose tolerance was tightened by [6836f4f50a8d](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/commit/6836f4f50a8d8abf7e0d0b1a92a8e5c5c26cff45). That explains the changed count without requiring a new underlying regression.

**Suspected cause and next diagnostics**

The recent Python 3.12 failure uses released NumPy 2.5.3, not NumPy `main`. The system OpenBLAS package remains `0.3.20+ds-1` across the historical failures, and the same runner image has both passing and failing examples. A runner-dependent OpenBLAS kernel problem is therefore a candidate. Region is only a correlation: the logs do not identify the CPU model or selected OpenBLAS kernel, so neither a specific CPU nor a recent fleet change is established.

body:
#### Reference issue
Closes gh-23990

#### What does this implement/fix?
The `griddata` documentation did not mention that interpolation results can differ between machines, even with the same input data. I added a note to the docstring explaining that `griddata` uses Delaunay triangulation for the `linear` and `cubic` methods. On a rectilinear grid, the triangulation is not unique because the four corners of a rectangle are co-circular. The diagonal selected can therefore vary due to floating-point rounding across platforms or Qhull versions, which can lead to slightly different interpolated values. For data on a regular grid, the documentation now points users to `RegularGridInterpolator` (or `interpn`) to avoid this triangulation ambiguity.

title: BUG: sparse: fix float32 upcast to float64 in sparse.linalg.norm

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
#### Reference issue
Fixes #26281.

#### What does this implement/fix?
In PR #24121, `np.can_cast(x.dtype, float)` was added to safely upcast integers to `float` (which numpy resolves to `float64`) to prevent overflow when calculating the matrix or vector norms. 

However, since `np.can_cast(np.float32, float)` is `True`, this had the unintended side effect of incorrectly upcasting `float32` sparse inputs to `float64` for norms evaluated via `abs(x).sum(...)` (e.g. `ord=1`, `ord=np.inf`, etc.). Interestingly, `np.can_cast(np.complex64, float)` is `False`, so complex types correctly avoided this upcast and retained single precision.

This PR modifies the dtype check to explicitly look for integer and boolean types (`x.dtype.kind in 'bui'`) instead of any castable type, mirroring how `numpy.linalg.norm` accurately preserves precision for `float32` inputs.

#### Additional information
Added a regression test to `TestVsNumpyNorm` to ensure the output dtype of `scipy.sparse.linalg.norm` exactly matches that of `numpy.linalg.norm` for single and double precision floats and complexes across all order combinations.

title: BUG: stats.yeojohnson: return lmbda=1 for arbitrary constant inputs

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
#### Description

This PR fixes an issue in `scipy.stats.yeojohnson_normmax` where passing a constant 1D array results in arbitrary and extreme optimal λ values.

When applying the Yeo-Johnson transform to constant data, the variance is zero regardless of the λ applied. Because the log-likelihood calculation includes the logarithm of the variance, that part of the equation evaluates to negative infinity (making the likelihood undefined) for any λ. The optimizer ends up chasing floating-point rounding errors during these operations, leading to silent numerical explosions. For example:

* Constant `4` →λ≈76.7, transformed values ≈ `5e51`
* Constant `1000` → transformed values ≈ `3e100`
* Constant `-3` →λ≈−43.5

To resolve this safely, this PR generalizes the existing fallback mechanism. Previously, `yeojohnson_normmax` explicitly checked for arrays of all zeros and returned λ=1. This check has now been broadened to apply to any constant array.

Returning λ=1 is the safest default, as it reduces the transform to the identity function, leaving the constant inputs unchanged. While the sibling function `boxcox` raises an error on constant data, SciPy already has backward-compatibility tests relying on `yeojohnson_normmax([0, 0, 0])` returning a finite value. Expanding this fallback fixes the bug without introducing breaking changes.

(Note for maintainers: If the preference is to align strictly with `boxcox` and raise a `ValueError` for all constant arrays, including zeros, I am happy to update the PR).

#### Modifications & Testing

* Updated `yeojohnson_normmax` to check for equality against the first element instead of zero.
* Verified that `nan_policy='omit'` works seamlessly: since NaNs are already stripped before the constant check, constant arrays with NaNs naturally return λ=1 without requiring extra logic.
* Added parameterized tests for `yeojohnson` and `yeojohnson_normmax` covering various constants (`-3`, `0.001`, `1`, `4`, `1000`).
* Added tests asserting that the transformed array is identical to the input array (tested on cases without NaNs).
* Added a test verifying that λ=1 is correctly returned for a constant input containing a NaN.

#### Reference issue
Closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/18969
Builds on PR #21620, which is currently open.

#### What does this implement/fix?
This PR is a continuation of the work done in PR #21620, which introduced the
`scipy.sparse.linalg.cond1est` function, and the
`scipy.sparse.linalg.rinvnormest` function.

Changes herein:
- Retain `cond1est`
- Remove `rinvnormest` from `scipy.sparse.linalg`
- Refactor `rinvnormest` to `normest_inv` in `scipy.sparse.linalg.SuperLU`


#### Additional information
The `cond1est` function estimates the condition number of a sparse matrix in the
1-norm, which is defined as the product of the 1-norm of the matrix, and the
1-norm of its inverse. This PR slightly changes the internal functionality of
`cond1est` by computing the exact 1-norm of the matrix with
`sparse.linalg.norm`, as opposed to the estimate `sparse.linalg.onenormest`.
This PR also adds input checking to `cond1est`, and updates the docstring.

This PR removes the `scipy.sparse.linalg.rinvnormest` function from
`scipy.sparse.linalg`, but retains the functionality in the
`scipy.sparse.linalg.SuperLU` class. There is no analogous function in either
numpy or scipy for dense matrices, so it is unnecessary to expose it at the top
level of `scipy.sparse.linalg`.

This PR renames the `SuperLU.rinvnormest` method to `normest_inv`, which better
reflects the mathematical syntax ``norm(inv(A))``. The method now returns the
norm itself rather than its reciprocal. The API has also been updated to accept
either the integer `1` or float `np.inf` as the norm order, as opposed to
a string argument.

Finally, this PR adds extensive tests for the `normest_inv` and `cond1est` for
sparse matrices of various sizes, densities, and data types. The tests also
include checks for the correct return types and values, as well as error
handling for invalid inputs.

There is an additional script in
`scipy/sparse/linalg/_dev_scripts/check_normcond_behavior.py` that demonstrates
the existing behavior of `np.linalg.norm`, `np.linalg.cond`,
`scipy.linalg.norm`, and `scipy.sparse.linalg.onenormest`.
